title: Holi: the festival of colors
hookLine: Prahlad walks out of the fire unharmed; the next morning everyone throws color and nobody is a stranger
carry: bhakti walks out of the fire
tomorrow: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva
last: FROM DARKNESS, LEAD ME TO LIGHT.

lines: A PILE GROWS AT THE CROSSROADS.
cards: In the days before Holi, in many villages and city lanes, a pile starts to grow at a crossroads or an open patch of ground: branches, scrap wood, cakes of dried cow dung, whatever people can spare.

Sometimes a small figure is set on top. On the full-moon night, people gather around it at dusk, walk around it, offer grain and coconut, and then light it. Tomorrow these streets will be pink and green.
Tonight belongs to the fire, and the fire has a name.

teach.b: The bonfire is called Holika Dahan, the burning of Holika. The story behind it belongs to a demon king, Hiranyakashipu, who has made himself almost impossible to kill and demands to be worshiped.
His own son, Prahlad, a boy, won't do it. Prahlad is devoted to Vishnu, and says so. The Bhagavata Purana tells how the king tried again and again to destroy his son, and how every attempt failed.
The version Holi remembers adds the king's sister, Holika. In the story people tell, fire could not harm her, and she sits in a blazing pyre with the boy in her lap, to burn him.

teach.h: THE FIRE TAKES HOLIKA, NOT THE BOY.
teach.b: Instead, the fire takes her, and Prahlad walks out unharmed, still saying the name of Vishnu. That's the teaching Holi keeps alive: bhakti, loving trust in God, is safer than any power a king can hold.
In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says it plainly: my devotee never perishes. So the bonfire is a remembering: the pride and cruelty burned, the trusting child safe.

teach.h: BHAKTI WALKS OUT OF THE FIRE.
teach.b: Then comes the morning after the full moon of Phalguna, at the edge of spring, when the streets fill with gulal, colored powder, and water.
Neighbors who don't speak, bosses and workers, old and young, all get the same handful of pink on the face.
Many people use Holi to visit, forgive, and start again, and many read the colors through Prahlad's own teaching in the Bhagavata: the Lord lives in every being, so nobody stands above anybody else.

how: On the full-moon night of Phalguna, many Hindus light the Holika Dahan bonfire and circle it with offerings; the next morning they play with colored powder and water, visit friends and family, and share sweets like gujiya.

o: a harvest feast where new grain is first cooked
the spring festival of color after a bonfire

games.q: the fire and the colors — tap the pairs.

s: Holika Dahan remembers that devotion came through the fire
the fire took Holika, and Prahlad walked out still saying Vishnu's name.
in the story, the fire burns Prahlad and spares Holika
the fire takes Holika, and Prahlad walks out unharmed.
the colors are thrown on the full-moon night itself
the bonfire is lit on the full-moon night; the colors come the next morning.

games.q: you're Prahlad. your father, the king, demands that you worship him instead of Vishnu. what do you do?
o: keep your devotion and say so.
games.why: he keeps his devotion openly, through every attempt on his life, and walks out of the fire unharmed. that's bhakti: trust in God over any king.

practice: On Holika Dahan, families walk around the fire and offer grain. Sit, and on each slow breath out, say Vishnu's name as many devotees do, Om Namo Narayanaya, or, if you don't pray, the word trust.
Then bring to mind one small grudge you've been carrying and picture it as a stick of wood. Lay it on the fire. You don't have to forgive anyone yet; just let your hands be empty.

wordCard.voice: Holi. A bonfire for Prahlad, the devoted child the fire couldn't take, then a spring morning of color when everyone looks the same.

orig.note: Hindi and Sanskrit: holikā + dahana (burning). the bonfire on the night before the colors.

carryVoice: Your line: bhakti walks out of the fire. Tomorrow, a night nobody sleeps. That's day six hundred seventy-four.
